query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys reported to date commonly contain both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Induction-melted Al- and Mg-rich alloys reached densities of 2.64–2.75 g/cm3 but all had complex structures; Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 combined a density of 3.91 g/cm3 with 911 HV hardness and oxidation resistance at 700 and 900 °C; compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd showed region-dependent compression, plasticity, and corrosion behavior; and reported AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys contained a primary BCC constituent together with intermetallic compounds, with x = 1.0 showing the best property combination in that series. Prior studies have emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, whereas interfacial segregation, interfacial energy, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance remain insufficiently studied. The design must retain a density below 6 g/cm3 and address performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds. Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state, what single intervention hypothesis could improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance? State the intervention, its proposed causal mechanism, quantitative or directional predictions relative to the as-processed baseline, the composition and operating or test boundaries, the prior experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of Cr to a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy will improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy
generation.mechanism: The addition of Cr promotes the formation of a dense oxidation film, which improves the high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount of Cr to be added and the potential effects on the alloy's microstructure and properties

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with varying amounts of Cr and test their mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Cr does not improve the combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance of the alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties.
